newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian cocoa exporters await end of tax squeeze.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian cocoa exporters await end of tax squeeze.

text.p: Ivorian exporters' cash flow will pick up along with cocoa arrivals from January as shorter export tax payment periods set in October return to normal, say forwarders.
"The Ministry of Finance imposed shorter periods to balance budgets for the year but they will end on December 31," said one forwarder.
Cocoa and coffee taxes usually fall due 20 days after shipments are declared to customs. Between October 24 to December 31 the period was cut to three days.

"Exporters cannot call in bills in three days and some banks are not helping out with bridging finance," said one forwarder. "Forwarders have had to pay on behalf of some clients and then fight their banks for reimbursement."
Exporters said the tax rule had not delayed exports. They put stocks warehouse stocks around Abidjan and San Pedro ports at 150,000 tonnes.
"There has been a standing stock of about 100,000 tonnes but levels are still below normal for this time of year," said one forwarder. "Drying has delayed arrivals along with demand patterns."
Others estimated cocoa in the pipeline from the farmgate downwards ahead of stronger early 1997 arrivals to be in a wide 300,000 tonne range.
Warehouse stocks next to ports would slip back to about 100,000 tonnes after shipments now being loaded depart, forwarders said.
Ships had wasted time in port approaches because of a requirement to announce berthings five days in advance. World Bank port efficiency recommendations include cutting the period to three days.
"Two days would make more sense. Some logistical flexibility is needed," said another forwarder.
